analogy.p: Imagine a marshal at the side of a road counting runners who pass in a steady line. The **frequency** is how many runners pass the marshal each second, the **wavelength** is the gap between neighbouring runners, and the **speed** of the line is the number passing per second multiplied by the gap: v = f × λ. If the starter sends runners out faster (higher frequency) but the line still moves at the same speed, the gaps must shrink, just as the ripple wavelength shrinks when you speed up the dipper. The analogy breaks down because runners carry themselves along, whereas in a wave the water or string only moves up and down and the energy, not the material, travels.

bullets: You must be able to **describe a method** for finding the **speed of water ripples** and of **waves on a string**, giving apparatus, measurements and the equation used.
You must be able to **measure wavelength accurately** by measuring across **several wavelengths** and dividing, instead of measuring a single wavelength.
You must be able to find **frequency** from a signal generator, a strobe light or by counting the waves that pass a point in a measured time.
You must know the equation **v = f × λ** and its rearrangements, with units: **m/s**, **Hz** and **m**.
You must be able to name the **independent, dependent and control variables** for each method.
You must be able to comment on **suitability of the apparatus**, sources of error, **uncertainty**, improvements and **safety**.
Link: the required practical applies the wave equation from *Wave properties and the wave equation* to real measurements.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 required practical 8 asks you to **make observations to identify the suitability of apparatus to measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank (a fluid) and waves in a solid (a string or elastic cord), and take appropriate measurements**. You must then use **wave speed = frequency × wavelength** to calculate the speed. The practical is examined as a method question, a calculation, a variables question, a graph question and an evaluation of accuracy and safety, so you need to understand the reasons behind every step and not only the order of the steps.

bullets: **v = f × λ** (wave speed in m/s; frequency in Hz; wavelength in m).
Rearranged: **f = v ÷ λ** and **λ = v ÷ f**.
**Period T = 1 ÷ f** (seconds); a 20 Hz wave has a period of 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05 s.
**1 Hz = 1 wave per second**; **1 kHz = 1000 Hz**.
If frequency is **doubled** at constant speed, wavelength is **halved**, because λ = v ÷ f.
Convert **cm to m** (divide by 100) and **mm to m** (divide by 1000) **before** substituting.
The wave **speed** depends on the **medium** (and, for water waves, the **depth**), not on the frequency of the source.
core.h: Recap: the wave equation and frequency
core.p: Every measurement in this practical feeds into one equation: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, written **v = f λ**. The **frequency** is the number of complete waves that pass a point (or are produced by the source) each second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz is one wave per second. The **wavelength** is the distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave, for example crest to crest, measured in **metres**. The **period** T is the time for one complete wave, and **T = 1 ÷ f**. Because the **source** sets the frequency, the frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the dipper or vibration generator that makes it.

bullets: **Shallow water** (about 5 mm): the waves are slower and easier to see, and keeping the **depth constant** keeps the wave speed constant.
**Straight dipper bar**: produces **plane (straight) waves** that are easy to measure; a single ball dipper produces circular waves.
**Variable-speed motor**: allows the **frequency** of the waves to be changed.
**Lamp above the tank**: lights the water so the pattern is projected onto the screen.
**White screen or paper under the tank**: shows the shadow pattern of the wavefronts clearly.
**Stroboscope (strobe light)**: flashes at a set frequency so that the moving waves appear to **stand still** when the flash frequency equals the wave frequency.
**Level tank** (checked with a spirit level or by adjusting the feet): the depth of water is then the same everywhere, so wavelength is not changed by depth differences.
**Metre rule or ruler** on or beside the tank: gives a real-world scale for measuring wavelength.
core.h: Ripple tank apparatus: what each part does
core.p: A **ripple tank** is a shallow, flat-bottomed tray with a transparent base, filled with water to a depth of only a few millimetres. A **motor-driven dipper** (a bar or a small ball that touches the surface) vibrates up and down to make waves on the water. A **lamp** above the tank shines light down through the water onto a **white screen or sheet of paper** below. Because the crests and troughs act like tiny lenses, they change how much light reaches each place on the screen, so the wave pattern is seen as **bright and dark lines**. Each part of the apparatus has a job, and exam questions often ask you to say why it is needed.

bullets: **1.** Place the tank on a bench, check it is **level**, and add water to a depth of about **5 mm**. Place the lamp above it and a white screen or paper below.
**2.** Lower the **dipper** until it just touches the water surface, and switch on the **motor** to produce plane waves.
**3.** Adjust the **motor speed** until a clear pattern of bright and dark lines appears on the screen.
**4.** Use a **strobe light** (adjust its frequency until the pattern appears to stand still) or take a **video or photo** so that the waves can be measured without moving.
**5.** Place a **ruler** against the pattern and measure the distance across a **known number of bright lines**, for example **10 lines**, which spans **9 wavelengths**.
**6.** Calculate the wavelength: **λ = measured distance ÷ number of wavelengths**, and convert to metres.
**7.** Find the **frequency** (from the strobe setting, the motor control, or by counting waves in a time), then calculate **v = f × λ**.
**8.** Repeat at several frequencies and calculate a **mean speed**.
core.h: Ripple tank method, step by step
core.p: The method is the same each time, and a good answer lists the steps in a sensible order and gives a reason for the important ones. Start by making sure the apparatus is set up safely and that the water depth is constant, then generate waves, freeze or capture the pattern, measure the wavelength over several waves, find the frequency and finally calculate the speed. Repeating at different frequencies and calculating a mean speed improves reliability.

bullets: Measuring **across 10 bright lines** gives **9 wavelengths**; count the **gaps**, not the lines.
Measure from the **same point** on each line (for example the centre of the bright line) so the distance is accurate.
The ruler has a **resolution of 1 mm**, so the uncertainty in one reading is about **± 0.5 mm** at each end; spreading this over several wavelengths reduces the **percentage uncertainty**.
Put the ruler **on the screen at the level of the pattern** and look straight down, to avoid **parallax error**.
If the shadow is magnified, **scale the measurement**: real distance = measured distance ÷ magnification, where magnification = size of the tank on the screen ÷ real size of the tank.
Taking a **photograph with a ruler in the tank** is more accurate because the ruler and waves are magnified equally.
**Repeat the measurement** at different places on the screen and calculate a **mean** to reduce random error.
core.p: The wavelength of ripples is only a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres, so measuring a single wavelength with a ruler gives a large **percentage uncertainty**. The better method is to measure across **many wavelengths** and divide. If you measure across **n bright lines**, the distance covers **(n − 1) wavelengths**, because there is one gap fewer than the number of lines. Examiners often test this counting point, and it is the most common arithmetic slip in the practical. The pattern on the screen may also be **magnified**, because the lamp is close to the tank, so measurements must be scaled back to the real size of the tank.

bullets: **Frequency = number of waves ÷ time**, for example 120 waves in 10 s gives 12 Hz.
With a **strobe**, increase the flash rate slowly until the pattern first appears to **freeze**; this gives the frequency.
With a **video**, step through frame by frame and count the frames for one wave, or time several waves.
Counting by eye over a **short time** is difficult and has a large **reaction-time error**, so count over a **longer time** and divide.
The **motor dial** may only give an approximate frequency, so checking with a strobe improves **accuracy**.
**Frequency is a count per second**, so make sure you divide by the **time in seconds**.
The frequency is set by the **source**, so it does not change as the waves travel across the tank.
core.h: Finding the frequency of the ripples
core.p: The frequency of the waves equals the frequency at which the dipper vibrates. There are three ways to find it, and a good evaluation compares their accuracy. The most direct is to read the frequency from the **motor controller or signal generator**, if it has a display. A **stroboscope** can also be used: the strobe flashes at a set number of flashes per second, and when the waves appear to stand still the strobe frequency matches the wave frequency (or a simple multiple of it, which is why you start with a low strobe frequency). Lastly the frequency can be found by **counting** how many waves pass a point in a set time.

bullets: Always **convert the wavelength to metres** before multiplying: 1.5 cm = **0.015 m**.
Example: f = 16 Hz and λ = 0.015 m gives **v = 16 × 0.015 = 0.24 m/s**.
If the speeds from different frequencies are close, the results are **repeatable**; large differences suggest a measurement error or a change in depth.
Calculate a **mean speed** from your repeats and give it to a suitable number of **significant figures** (the same as your least precise measurement).
Higher frequency means **shorter wavelength**: this is an **inverse proportion** (λ ∝ 1/f when v is constant).
A graph of **λ against f** is a **curve** (inverse); a graph of **λ against 1/f** is a **straight line** through the origin.
The **gradient** of λ against 1/f has units of **m/s**, because λ ÷ (1/f) = λ × f.
core.h: Calculating wave speed and checking the result
core.p: Once the wavelength and frequency have been found, the speed follows from **v = f × λ**. For ripples in shallow water of a fixed depth, the speed is approximately **constant** whatever the frequency, so if the frequency is increased the wavelength gets smaller and the **product f × λ stays about the same**. Checking that your values of speed agree for different frequencies is a good test of whether your measurements are reliable. Plotting **wavelength against 1/frequency** gives a straight line through the origin, and the **gradient is the wave speed**.

bullets: **Signal generator**: produces an alternating signal of **known, adjustable frequency** (displayed on the dial).
**Vibration generator**: converts the signal into **vibrations** of the end of the string, at the same frequency as the signal.
**Pulley and masses**: keep the **tension** in the string **constant** (and let you change it if needed).
**Metre rule**: used to measure the distance occupied by the loops.
**Clamp and stand**: hold the vibration generator and pulley firmly so the apparatus does not move.
**Eye protection and a tray or box** under the masses: protect against the string breaking or masses falling.
The waves on the string are **transverse**: the string moves **at right angles** to the direction the energy travels.
core.h: Waves on a string or elastic cord: apparatus
core.p: The second part of the practical investigates waves in a **solid**, usually a **string, rope or elastic cord**. One end of the string is attached to a **vibration generator** which is driven by a **signal generator** that sets the frequency. The other end is held in a clamp or passed over a pulley with a **mass hanger** that provides the **tension**. As the generator vibrates the end of the string, **transverse waves** travel along the string. At certain frequencies the waves reflect from the fixed end and combine with the incoming waves to form a clear pattern of **loops** that appears to stand still, which is easy to measure.

bullets: **1.** Set up the vibration generator, string, pulley and masses and **clamp them securely**; keep the mass and string length the same throughout.
**2.** Connect the vibration generator to the **signal generator** and switch on at a low frequency.
**3.** **Increase the frequency slowly** until a clear pattern of loops appears with the string vibrating strongly.
**4.** Read the **frequency** from the signal generator.
**5.** Measure the length of the string covered by **several loops**, for example **4 loops**, using a metre rule.
**6.** Work out the wavelength: **one loop is half a wavelength**, so **λ = 2 × (length of the loops ÷ number of loops)**. For 4 loops, λ = length ÷ 2.
**7.** Calculate **v = f × λ** and repeat at **other frequencies** that give clear patterns.
**8.** Calculate the **mean speed**; it should be the **same** at each frequency because the tension and string are unchanged.
core.p: With the string tensioned, the aim is to find frequencies at which a **clear, steady pattern of loops** is seen, then measure the length of the loops and use the signal generator frequency. The pattern forms best at particular frequencies, so you vary the frequency slowly and watch the string. Once a clear pattern is found, the measurement is the same each time, and results at several frequencies can be compared.

bullets: **Node**: a point on the string that **does not move**; **antinode**: the point in the middle of a loop with **maximum movement**.
**Distance between adjacent nodes = λ ÷ 2**; so **one loop is half a wavelength**.
**Two loops = one complete wavelength**.
For **n loops** occupying a length L: **λ = 2L ÷ n**.
Example: 3 loops over 0.45 m gives λ = 2 × 0.45 ÷ 3 = **0.30 m**.
The end next to the vibration generator moves very little compared with the loops, so it acts like a **node**.
Measuring across **several loops** reduces the **percentage uncertainty** just like measuring across several wavelengths in the ripple tank.
The pattern appears only at **particular frequencies** where the string fits a whole number of loops.
core.h: Reading wavelength from a stationary pattern
core.p: The pattern of loops on the string is called a **stationary (standing) wave**. It is formed when a wave travelling along the string is **reflected** at the far end and **overlaps** with the incoming wave. In the pattern some points, called **nodes**, do not move at all, while the points halfway between them, called **antinodes** (the middle of each loop), vibrate with the largest amplitude. The key fact for this practical is that the distance between **two neighbouring nodes** is **half a wavelength**, so **one loop equals λ/2**. This is easy to confuse with the wavelength of a travelling wave, and examiners expect you to apply it correctly.

bullets: **Ripple tank, independent variable:** the **frequency** of the dipper (motor speed).
**Ripple tank, dependent variable:** the **wavelength** of the ripples (and the calculated speed).
**Ripple tank, control variables:** **depth of water** (the main one), the same tank and water, and a level tank.
**String, independent variable:** the **frequency** set on the signal generator.
**String, dependent variable:** the **wavelength** (found from the length of the loops), and so the speed.
**String, control variables:** the **tension** (same mass on the hanger), the **length** and **type of string**.
If the **depth** or **tension** changed, the **speed** would change, so it must be controlled.
Valid conclusion: **wave speed is constant** for a given medium and conditions while frequency and wavelength change.
core.p: Examination questions often ask you to identify the **independent**, **dependent** and **control** variables, and to explain why the control variables must be kept the same so the test is a **fair test**. In both methods you change the frequency and observe the effect on the wavelength, and you must make sure nothing else that could affect the wave speed changes. If a control variable changed, you would not know whether a change in wavelength was due to the frequency or to the other change, so the results would not be **valid**.

bullets: **Percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty ÷ measured value) × 100**. Measuring 1.5 cm with ± 0.1 cm gives **6.7%**; measuring 12.0 cm across 8 wavelengths with ± 0.1 cm gives only **0.83%**.
**Parallax error** when reading the ruler: look **directly above** the scale, or use a photograph with a ruler included.
**Magnified shadow**: scale the measurement using a known length such as the tank width.
**Reaction-time error** when counting waves: count for a **longer time** or use a **video**.
**Water depth varies** if the tank is not level: use a **spirit level** and adjust the feet.
**String sags or tension changes**: use a pulley and a fixed mass, and check the string is horizontal.
**Frequency read from a dial** may be inaccurate: check with a **strobe** or a **frequency meter**.
**Improve reliability** by **repeating** and calculating a **mean**, and by testing **more frequencies**.
core.h: Uncertainty, errors and improving the experiment
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to say why a result may be inaccurate and how the method could be improved. The main sources of error come from **measuring small distances** and **finding the frequency**. Reducing **percentage uncertainty** is done by measuring **larger distances** or using more precise instruments. Mark schemes reward specific improvements that link to a particular error rather than vague comments like 'be more careful'.

bullets: **Hazard:** mains-powered lamp, motor and leads near **water**. **Risk:** electric shock. **Control:** keep **leads and sockets away from the water**, mop up spills immediately, and switch off before adjusting equipment.
**Hazard:** water on the floor. **Risk:** slipping. **Control:** wipe spills quickly and keep walkways clear.
**Hazard:** a **strobe light**. **Risk:** can trigger seizures in people with **photosensitive epilepsy**. **Control:** use only for short times, warn others, and avoid use by anyone at risk.
**Hazard:** **hanging masses**. **Risk:** can fall and hurt feet or the string can break. **Control:** place a **tray, box or sand** under the masses and use only the necessary mass.
**Hazard:** a string under tension that **snaps**. **Risk:** eye injury. **Control:** wear **eye protection** and stand back.
**Hazard:** a **hot lamp**. **Risk:** burns. **Control:** allow it to cool before handling.
**Vibration generator** may be hot or vibrate off the bench: **clamp it** firmly and do not leave it running.
core.p: A risk assessment states the **hazard**, the **risk** (the harm that could result) and the **control measure**. In this practical there are two main hazards: water near electrical equipment, and the stroboscope and hanging masses. Always give all three parts of the answer, because 'be careful' scores no marks.

bullets: **Ripple tank:** waves are **slow** (about tens of cm per second) and the **wavelength is a few mm to cm**, so they can be measured with a ruler.
**Strobe light:** makes the **fast-moving pattern appear still**, so measurements are possible.
**Vibration generator and signal generator:** provide a **known, accurate frequency**.
**String:** the **loops** are easy to see and measure; the speed is typically several metres per second.
**Metre rule:** suitable for measuring loops of tens of centimetres; a **ruler with mm divisions** is suitable for ripples.

**Not suitable for light or sound in air:** the speed of **sound is about 340 m/s** and light is **3 × 10⁸ m/s**, which makes the wavelength and period impossible to measure directly with this equipment.
A **video camera or phone** with a ruler in view is a useful improvement for both methods.
core.p: The specification asks you to identify the **suitability of apparatus**, which means deciding which equipment gives measurements that are good enough for the job. The ripple tank is ideal for **water waves** because waves are slow and large enough to see, and the pattern can be made to appear stationary. The **string** is ideal for waves in a solid because the vibration generator gives an accurate known frequency and the loops are large enough to measure with a metre rule. Neither apparatus is suitable for **sound** or **light**, because those waves are far too fast and have wavelengths too short to be seen or measured with these methods.

bullets: **Table headings** must include **quantity and unit**, for example 'Frequency (Hz)' and 'Wavelength (m)'.
**Conclusion:** 'as the frequency increases the wavelength decreases, and the wave speed stays the same'.
**Use data:** 'at 10 Hz λ = 0.024 m, at 20 Hz λ = 0.012 m, both giving v = 0.24 m/s'.
On a graph of **λ against 1/f** the points lie on a **straight line through the origin**, showing λ is **inversely proportional** to f.
The **gradient** equals the **wave speed**; calculate it using a **large triangle** that covers more than half of the line.
A **point far from the line** is an **anomaly**: check it, repeat, and exclude it from the mean if justified.
Say whether results are **repeatable** (similar values on repeats) and **accurate** (close to the true or expected value).
core.p: After taking measurements, you should present results in a **table** with units in the column headings, calculate the speed for each frequency and then look for patterns. A conclusion in the exam must be **linked to the data** and use correct scientific language. For this practical, the key conclusions are that **as frequency increases, wavelength decreases**, and that the **speed stays (approximately) constant** for a given medium and conditions. You should also be ready to **plot a graph** and use its gradient.

bullets: **Wave properties:** the practical measures **frequency, wavelength and speed** directly, so it supports the wave equation.
**Refraction:** if you place a **flat glass or plastic block** in the tank to make a shallow region, the waves **slow down** and the **wavelength shortens**, while the **frequency stays the same**.
**Transverse waves:** the waves on the string are **transverse**; ripples on water are mostly described as **transverse**.
**Waves transfer energy, not matter:** a floating cork **bobs up and down** but does not travel across the tank with the waves.
**Higher tier:** be ready to explain, using **v = fλ**, why changing the frequency at constant speed changes the wavelength.
**Sound and light:** for these waves the same equation applies with different speeds, for example **v = 340 m/s** for sound in air.
**Maths skills:** unit conversions, means, percentage uncertainty, rearranging equations and gradients of straight-line graphs.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier thinking
core.p: The ripple tank and string practical connects with several other parts of the Waves topic. The wave equation is used again for **sound**, **light** and **the electromagnetic spectrum**, where the speed is different but the equation is unchanged. The ripple tank is also the standard way to demonstrate **reflection and refraction** of waves, because slower waves in shallow water show the effect of changing depth. For higher marks, link the **measurements** to the **ideas**: the source sets the frequency, the medium sets the speed, and the wavelength follows from the two.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark):** give the equipment and its job, for example 'stroboscope: makes the waves appear to stand still' or 'signal generator: sets the frequency'.

**Describe a method (4 to 6 marks):** set up the tank level with shallow water; produce waves with the dipper; use a strobe to freeze the pattern; measure across several wavelengths with a ruler and divide; find the frequency; calculate v = f × λ; repeat and take a mean. Use ordered, separate points.
**Why measure across several wavelengths? (2 marks):** it reduces the percentage uncertainty because the same ruler error is spread over a larger distance (1), so the wavelength is more accurate (1).
**Calculation (2 to 3 marks):** write the equation (1), substitute with consistent units (1), give the answer with the unit (1). Convert cm or mm to m first.
**Stationary wave on a string:** quote that one loop is half a wavelength and that λ = 2 × length ÷ number of loops.
**Variables:** name independent (frequency), dependent (wavelength), and at least one control with a reason (depth or tension affects the speed).

**Evaluate (3 to 4 marks):** give a specific source of error (parallax, reaction time, magnified shadow, uneven depth), say how it affects the result, and give a matching improvement (use a photograph with a ruler, count over longer, use a strobe, check level).
**Safety (2 to 3 marks):** hazard + risk + control, for example water and mains electricity so keep leads away; strobe and photosensitive epilepsy so use briefly; masses so place a tray below.
**Graph questions:** λ against 1/f is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is the wave speed; use a large triangle and give units.
**Command words:** 'describe' = steps in order; 'explain' = give the reason using 'because'; 'calculate' = show working; 'evaluate' = strengths, weaknesses and a judgement.

mistakes.r: Measure across several wavelengths (for example 10 lines = 9 wavelengths) and divide, to reduce the percentage uncertainty.
mistakes.w: I measured the wavelength of one wave with a ruler and used that.

mistakes.r: The distance across 10 lines contains 9 wavelengths; count the gaps between lines, not the lines.
mistakes.w: Ten bright lines are ten wavelengths, so I divided the distance by 10.

mistakes.r: The distance between adjacent nodes (one loop) is half a wavelength; two loops make one wavelength.
mistakes.w: On the string, the distance between two nodes is one wavelength.

mistakes.r: Convert the wavelength to metres first (divide cm by 100), or give the speed in cm/s.
mistakes.w: I used the wavelength in cm in v = f λ and gave the speed in m/s.

mistakes.r: Frequency is the number of waves per second (waves ÷ time in seconds), measured in hertz.
mistakes.w: Frequency is the number of waves.

mistakes.r: Waves transfer energy, not matter: the water moves up and down about a fixed position.
mistakes.w: The water travels across the tank with the wave.

mistakes.r: Depth or tension affects wave speed, so it must be controlled; only the frequency is changed.
mistakes.w: I changed the frequency and also the water depth (or the tension).

mistakes.r: The shadow may be magnified; scale the measurement using a known real length such as the tank width.
mistakes.w: The measurement on the screen is the real wavelength.

mistakes.r: The speed is set by the medium (and depth); increasing the frequency shortens the wavelength while the speed stays the same.
mistakes.w: Increasing the frequency makes the waves travel faster.

mistakes.r: State the hazard, risk and control: keep mains leads away from water to avoid electric shock; wipe spills to avoid slipping.
mistakes.w: Safety: be careful with the water.

summary: AQA 8463 required practical 8: you must make observations to identify the suitability of apparatus to measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank (fluid) and on a string (solid), take appropriate measurements and use wave speed = frequency × wavelength. It is examined through method, calculation, variables, graph, uncertainty and safety questions, so every step needs a reason.

terms.d: The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, for example crest to crest. Measured in metres.
The number of waves passing a point each second, or produced by a source each second. Measured in hertz (Hz).
The speed at which energy is transferred (the wave travels) through a medium. Measured in metres per second (m/s).
wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m), written v = f λ.
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; period = 1 ÷ frequency.
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one wave per second.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.
A shallow tray of water, with a dipper to make waves and a lamp and screen to show the pattern, used to investigate water waves.
A bar or small ball driven by a motor that touches the water surface and makes ripples at a set frequency.
A line joining points of a wave that are in step, for example the crest of a ripple; plane waves have straight wavefronts.
A light that flashes at an adjustable frequency, making a repeating motion appear to stand still when the flash rate matches the wave frequency.
An electronic device that produces an alternating signal of known, adjustable frequency to drive a vibration generator.
A device that vibrates at the frequency of the signal supplied to it, used to produce waves on a string.
A pattern of loops on a string formed when a wave and its reflection overlap; the pattern appears not to travel along the string.
A point on a stationary wave that does not move.
A point on a stationary wave, in the middle of a loop, where the movement is greatest.
The pulling force that stretches a string; keeping it constant keeps the wave speed constant.
(uncertainty ÷ measured value) × 100; measuring across several wavelengths reduces it.
A variable kept the same in an investigation so that the test is fair and only the independent variable affects the result.

worked.q: In a ripple tank, a student measures 12.0 cm across 9 bright lines on the screen (the screen shows the real size). The dipper frequency is 16 Hz. Calculate the speed of the waves. (4 marks)
steps: Nine bright lines span 8 wavelengths (count the gaps).

worked.q: A vibration generator drives a string at 50 Hz. A stationary wave with 4 loops covers 0.60 m of the string. Calculate the wavelength and the speed of the waves on the string. (3 marks)
steps: Each loop is half a wavelength, so 4 loops = 2 wavelengths.

worked.ans: Model answer: I level the tank, add about 5 mm of water and set the lamp above and a white screen below. I lower the dipper so it touches the water and switch on the motor to produce plane waves. I use a strobe light and adjust the flash rate until the pattern appears to stand still, noting the frequency. I measure across 10 bright lines with a ruler, which is 9 wavelengths, then divide by 9 and convert to metres to find the wavelength. I calculate the speed using wave speed = frequency × wavelength and repeat at other frequencies to find a mean. Measuring across several wavelengths gives a smaller percentage uncertainty because the same small ruler error is a smaller fraction of a bigger distance.
worked.q: Describe how you would use a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves, and explain why the measurement of wavelength is taken across several waves. (6 marks)
steps: Set up: level tank with about 5 mm of water, lamp above, white screen below.
Waves: lower the dipper to the surface and switch on the motor to make plane waves.
Freeze: use a strobe, adjusting its flash rate until the pattern appears stationary, and read the frequency.
Measure: place a ruler on the screen and measure the distance across 10 bright lines (9 wavelengths); divide to get λ and convert to metres.
Calculate: v = f × λ; repeat at other frequencies and find the mean speed.
Reason: measuring across several waves reduces the percentage uncertainty, because the uncertainty in reading the ruler is spread over a larger distance.
